intro: Lecce is the main city of the Salento, the heel of Italy, a few kilometres from the Adriatic. In the 16th and 17th centuries its builders carved the soft, golden local stone into churches and palaces so richly decorated that the style took the city’s name: Lecce Baroque.
famous: Lecce Baroque, above all the carved front of the Basilica di Santa Croce
A Roman amphitheatre half sunk in its main square
Papier-mâché saints, the cartapesta of its workshops
Pasticciotto for breakfast and caffè leccese with almond milk
facts: By the Messapians, before the Romans; the Romans called it Lupiae
The Adriatic, about 11 kilometres to the east
overview: Lecce is a city of honey-coloured stone. Almost the whole old town is built of pietra leccese, a limestone so soft when it is quarried that carvers could cover façades with flowers, fruit, cherubs, saints and monsters. Dozens of churches stand within a few minutes’ walk of each other in the small old town.

The old town, the part you ride through in Instant Lecce, lies inside a ring of broad avenues that replaced the city walls. Three gates survive: Porta Napoli to the north, Porta Rudiae to the west and Porta San Biagio to the south. Piazza Sant’Oronzo, with its Roman amphitheatre, is the centre; the Via Vittorio Emanuele II leads west from it to the closed square of the cathedral, and Santa Croce and the castle of Charles V lie to the north and east.
setting: Lecce lies in the south-east of Italy, in the region of Apulia, and is the capital of the province of Lecce. The Salento is a flat peninsula between the Adriatic and the Ionian Sea, covered with olive groves, vineyards and dry-stone walls. Brindisi lies about 40 kilometres to the north and Otranto about 40 kilometres to the south-east.

The climate is Mediterranean: long, hot and dry summers and mild winters. Since 2013 a bacterium, Xylella fastidiosa, has killed millions of the old olive trees of the Salento, and the landscape around the city is slowly being replanted.

history.title: Messapians and Romans
text: Before the Romans, the Messapians, a people of the heel of Italy, lived here and at Rudiae, just west of the town, where the Roman poet Ennius was later born. The Romans took the Salento in the 3rd century BC and made Lecce the town of Lupiae.

Under the emperors Lupiae built a theatre for about 5,000 people, in the time of Augustus, and in the 2nd century an amphitheatre for some 25,000. Legend says that Saint Oronzo, the city’s first bishop, was martyred here under Nero. Both Roman buildings lay hidden under the houses until the 20th century.

history.title: Counts, kings and the Ottoman threat
text: After Rome fell, Byzantines, Lombards and Saracens fought over the Salento, until the Normans took it in the 11th century and made Lecce the seat of a county. Its count Tancred became king of Sicily in 1189. In the following centuries the county passed through several noble families and then to the Kingdom of Naples, which Spain ruled from the early 16th century.

In 1480 an Ottoman fleet took Otranto, down the coast, and killed much of its population. Fear of the Turks shaped Lecce: in the 1530s Emperor Charles V had the castle rebuilt and new walls built around the town, and in 1548 the city raised Porta Napoli in his honour.

history.title: The Baroque city
text: In the century after 1550 the religious orders of the Counter-Reformation and Lecce’s noble families rebuilt the town in carved stone. Santa Croce took from 1549 to 1695 to finish; Giuseppe Zimbalo rebuilt the cathedral from 1659 and gave it its 70-metre bell tower. When the plague of 1656 spared Lecce, the city thanked Saint Oronzo and set his statue on a Roman column in the main square.

Lecce became part of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. Most of the walls came down in the 19th century and broad avenues took their place, while the new city grew outside them. In recent decades the restored old town and the beaches of the Salento have brought visitors from all over the world.

timeline: The Romans build the amphitheatre of Lupiae

Porta Rudiae is rebuilt in Baroque style

today: Lecce is the capital of its province and the seat of the University of Salento. Its economy rests on public services, the university, tourism, olive oil and wine from the Salento, such as Negroamaro and Salice Salentino. Stone carvers still work the pietra leccese, and papier-mâché workshops in the old town still make saints and nativity figures.

In the evening the whole town walks the streets between Piazza Sant’Oronzo and the cathedral. At the end of August the feast of Saint Oronzo fills the old town with lights, music and processions, and in summer the Salento dances the pizzica. The football club, US Lecce, plays in yellow and red at the Stadio Via del Mare.
